course.title: TypeScript Basics
course.description: Annotations, interfaces, unions, and narrowing — the type system that catches CRUD bugs before the code ever runs.

lessons.title: Annotating Primitives
lessons.explanation:
## Types on the label

TypeScript is JavaScript plus **annotations** — little `: type` labels on parameters, return values, and variables that the compiler checks before your code ever runs:

```ts
function applyDiscount(priceCents: number, percent: number): number {
  return Math.round(priceCents * (1 - percent / 100));
}

const sale: number = applyDiscount(2000, 25);  // 1500 ✓
applyDiscount('2000', 25);                      // ✗ compile error!
```

Line by line: `priceCents: number` declares what each parameter must be, and the `: number` after the parentheses declares what the function returns. The last line is the payoff — passing the *string* `'2000'` is caught **at compile time**, before the bug ships. In plain JavaScript, `'2000' * 0.75` would coerce and this exact mistake (form inputs are always strings!) is a classic CRUD bug.

The primitive types match JavaScript: `string`, `number`, `boolean` (plus `null`, `undefined`, `bigint`, `symbol`). Variables are usually **inferred** — `const n = 5` is already a `number` without an annotation — so annotate function boundaries, let inference handle locals.

One warning: the type `any` opts a value out of checking entirely. Every `any` is a hole in the safety net.

### Common mistakes

- Annotating everything. `const total: number = a + b` adds noise; inference knows.
- Reaching for `any` to silence an error instead of fixing the type.
- Forgetting types are erased at runtime: annotations check code, they don't convert values.

lessons.title: Interfaces & Object Types
Typed Arrays & Tuples
lessons.explanation:
## Many of one, or one of each

An **array type** is "any number of the same thing": `number[]`, `string[]`, `Task[]`. A **tuple** is the opposite — a fixed-length array where *each position* has its own type:

```ts
const scores: number[] = [90, 85, 72];
scores.push('98');              // ✗ compile error — strings can't get in

const entry: [string, number] = ['ada', 1200];   // tuple: name, then score
const [name, score] = entry;    // name: string, score: number — destructured with types intact

function minMax(nums: number[]): [number, number] {
  return [Math.min(...nums), Math.max(...nums)];
}
const [lo, hi] = minMax([3, 1, 4]);   // lo = 1, hi = 4
```

Line by line: the `number[]` annotation protects the array *forever* — every push, every assignment is checked, so a `number[]` can never secretly contain a string (the way JS arrays accumulate junk). The tuple `[string, number]` gives each slot a type: `entry[0]` is a string, `entry[1]` is a number, and `entry[2]` doesn't exist. Tuples are how typed functions return **two values at once** — `minMax` hands back a pair, and destructuring names the halves.

`Array<number>` is identical to `number[]` — two spellings, same type. Transforms keep types flowing: `nums.map(n => n * 2)` is still `number[]`, while `words.map(w => w.length)` turns `string[]` into `number[]`.

### Common mistakes

- Using an array where a tuple is meant: `number[]` says nothing about length or position meaning.
- Expecting tuple length to be enforced at runtime — like all types, it's compile-time only.

lessons.title: Function Types & Signatures
Union Types
lessons.explanation:
## Either this or that

A **union type** says a value is one of several possibilities: `string | number` is "a string OR a number". Unions model reality — ids that arrive as either kind, fields that may be null, statuses from a fixed menu:

```ts
function formatId(id: string | number): string {
  return '#' + id;              // ok: both sides support string concatenation
}

type Status = 'pending' | 'active' | 'done';   // a LITERAL union
function isFinished(s: Status): boolean {
  return s === 'done';
}
isFinished('done');     // ✓
isFinished('finished'); // ✗ compile error — not one of the three words
```

Line by line: with `id: string | number`, you may only do things valid for **every** member of the union — concatenation works for both, but `id.toUpperCase()` is an error (numbers can't). The literal union `Status` is even stricter: not "any string" but exactly those three spellings. This is the single highest-value TypeScript feature for CRUD apps — status fields, roles, and sort orders stop being stringly-typed guesswork, and a typo like `'finished'` dies at compile time.

To use member-specific operations you must **narrow** the union first (next lesson) — check which member you actually have.

### Common mistakes

- Typing a status as `string` when the real values are a known menu — you throw away the checking.
- Expecting `string | number` to let you call string methods — only common operations are allowed before narrowing.
- Writing `'pending' || 'active'` in a type position (that's value syntax; unions use `|`).

lessons.title: Narrowing
lessons.explanation:
## Proving which one you have

**Narrowing** is how you unlock member-specific operations on a union: write a runtime check the compiler understands, and inside that branch the type shrinks:

```ts
function describe(v: string | number[] | { count: number }): string {
  if (typeof v === 'string') {
    return v.toUpperCase();          // v: string here
  }
  if (Array.isArray(v)) {
    return v.length + ' items';      // v: number[] here
  }
  return v.count + ' counted';       // v: { count: number } — the only one left
}
```

Line by line: `typeof v === 'string'` is an ordinary runtime check, but TypeScript *understands* it — inside the branch, `v` is a plain `string`. `Array.isArray` narrows to the array member. And after both returns, the compiler has eliminated two of three members, so the last line can use `.count` with no check at all. The main narrowing tools:

- `typeof x === 'string' | 'number' | 'boolean'` — primitives
- `Array.isArray(x)` — arrays
- `x === null`, `x === undefined` — the empty members
- `'count' in x` — discriminating object shapes by property
- Truthiness `if (x)` — convenient but dangerous: it also eliminates `''` and `0`!

### Common mistakes

- `typeof x === 'object'` to detect your object member — `null` and arrays are also `'object'`.
- Truthiness-narrowing `string | null` with `if (s)` when the empty string is a legitimate value — use `s !== null`.
- Narrowing in one statement and using it in another where the compiler can't connect them.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Which is the correct TypeScript annotation for a function taking a string and returning a number?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: TypeScript annotations follow the name: `param: type` for each parameter, and `: returnType` after the parameter list. The other forms borrow syntax from Java, Python, and generics that TypeScript does not use this way.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Given `function double(n: number): number { return n * 2; }`, which call does the TypeScript compiler reject?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: `'21'` is a string, and the parameter demands a number — a compile-time error before the code runs. The compiler checks *types*, not *values*: negatives and fractions are perfectly valid numbers, so rejecting them would need runtime validation, not annotations.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Is the annotation needed in `const count: number = 3`?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: Initialized variables get their type inferred from the value, so the annotation is redundant noise. The convention: explicit types at API edges (parameters, return types, exported constants) where they document contracts; inference everywhere else.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: What does typing a parameter as `any` do?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: `any` is the opt-out: `x.definitely.not.there()` compiles without complaint when `x: any`. It silences errors by silencing *checking* — the bug just moves to runtime. (The safer "I don’t know yet" type is `unknown`, which forces you to narrow before use.)

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: At runtime, what remains of the annotation in `function greet(name: string) { ... }`?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: Compilation strips every type; the output is plain JavaScript. So annotations protect you from mistakes *in code the compiler can see* — data arriving at runtime (JSON bodies, form input) still needs real validation, because nothing enforces types at the boundary.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: In TypeScript, what is the type of `"id-" + 42`?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: TypeScript models JavaScript’s real semantics: string concatenation with `+` is legal and yields `string`. The checker is not a different language — it formalizes what JS does, and flags only the combinations that are *likely bugs* (like `"a" - 1`... which it rejects).

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: The annotations guide the compiler but the arithmetic is ordinary JavaScript: 2000 × 0.75 = 1500, and 999 × 0.9 = 899.1 rounds to 899. After compilation the type labels are gone; only the math remains.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: Three primitive annotations cover the whole signature; the boolean parameter drives the ternary. 'mug x3 (available)' and 'lamp x1 (sold out)'. Note `qty` is concatenated into a string — allowed, because `+` with a string operand stringifies, and TypeScript knows that rule too.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Export a function `square(n: number): number` that returns `n * n`, with both the parameter and return type annotated as `number`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: The annotated signature is a checked contract: callers cannot pass strings, and the body cannot return one. With `: number` declared, even `return String(n * n)` would be a compile error — return annotations catch bugs inside the function, not just at call sites.
hints: The body is one return statement; the exercise is the annotated signature.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Export a function `greet(name: string): string` that returns `'Hello, <name>!'` using a template literal.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: A `string` in, a `string` out — with the annotation, calling `greet(42)` is impossible to compile. In a JS codebase this function silently produces "Hello, 42!"; the type makes the mistake loud and early.
hints: Template literal with the parameter interpolated.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Export a function `isAdult(age: number): boolean` that returns whether `age >= 18`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: The `: boolean` return type documents that this is a predicate, and would flag a refactor that accidentally returned the age itself. Returning the comparison expression directly beats `if/else return true/false` — same value, less code.
hints: Return the comparison directly — it already evaluates to a boolean.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Export a function `celsiusToFahrenheit(c: number): number` that converts Celsius to Fahrenheit with the formula `c * 9 / 5 + 32`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: Unit conversions are where number-vs-string confusion hurts most: `"100" * 9 / 5 + 32` happens to work in JS by coercion, but `"100" + 32` elsewhere would concatenate. The annotation guarantees arithmetic semantics throughout. (−40 is the famous point where the scales meet.)
hints: Multiply by 9, divide by 5, add 32.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Export a function `repeatWord(word: string, times: number): string` that repeats the word with spaces between: `repeatWord('go', 3)` → `'go go go'`. Return `''` when times is 0.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: Two differently-typed parameters make the argument ORDER checkable: `repeatWord(3, "go")` is a compile error, where JavaScript would happily compute nonsense. fill/join handles the zero case for free: an empty array joins to the empty string.
hints: Array(times).fill(word).join(" ") — or a loop collecting into an array.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Export a function `minutesToSeconds(minutes: number): number` that converts minutes to seconds.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: Trivial body, meaningful signature: in a larger codebase, `number`-typed duration helpers chain safely (`minutesToSeconds(hoursToMinutes(2))`) while a stray string anywhere in the chain fails compilation instead of producing "260" (the string "2" + 60 coerced).
hints: Multiply by 60.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Export a function `formatScore(name: string, points: number): string` that returns `'<name>: <points> pts'`, e.g. `('Ada', 1200)` → `'Ada: 1200 pts'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: Interpolating a number into a template literal stringifies it — a *deliberate*, visible conversion at the display edge. TypeScript’s philosophy in miniature: keep data numeric for as long as math might happen; convert to string only when formatting.
hints: One template literal interpolating both parameters.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Export a function `applyDiscount(priceCents: number, percent: number): number` that returns the discounted price in cents, rounded with `Math.round`: `(2000, 25)` → `1500`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: The money-in-cents discipline from JavaScript carries over, now compiler-assisted: both inputs are guaranteed numeric, so the one remaining risk is the arithmetic itself (round exactly once, at the end). A `"25"` percent from a form field cannot reach this function uncoerced.
hints: Multiply by (1 - percent/100), then Math.round back to integer cents.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Export a function `clampVolume(v: number): number` that clamps a volume to the range 0-100.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: Types and runtime guards are complementary: `: number` ensures the *kind* of value at compile time, while the clamp constrains its *range* at runtime. Annotations never replace range checks — they just eliminate the whole category of wrong-type bugs first.
hints: Math.max enforces the floor, Math.min the ceiling.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Export a function `initialsOf(first: string, last: string): string` that returns the two upper-cased initials joined: `('ada', 'lovelace')` → `'AL'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: Indexing a `string` yields a `string` in TypeScript’s eyes, so the chain type-checks end to end. Two same-typed parameters are the one case annotations cannot help with argument order — naming (`first`, `last`) has to do that job.
hints: Index each string at 0, concatenate, upper-case once.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Export a function `hypotenuse(a: number, b: number): number` that returns the hypotenuse of a right triangle: `Math.sqrt(a * a + b * b)`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: Math helpers like `Math.sqrt` are themselves typed (`(x: number) => number` in the standard library declarations), so your annotations connect to a fully-typed chain — the standard library is the biggest interface you program against.
hints: Square both, add, Math.sqrt.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: Export a function `yesNo(value: boolean): string` that converts a boolean to `'yes'` or `'no'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: Boolean-to-label conversion belongs at the display edge, in one typed function — scattering `b ? "yes" : "no"` ternaries through templates is how inconsistent wording ("Yes", "y", "true") creeps into UIs.
hints: A single ternary.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions: This function's annotations are wrong — the logic treats `qty` as a number and returns a string, but the signature says otherwise. Fix ONLY the annotations so they describe what the code actually does (`qty: number`, returns `string`). Keep the body identical.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: Annotations are claims, and wrong claims are worse than none — every caller would be forced to pass a string qty and expect a number back. Reading the body to determine the true types is a daily TypeScript skill: the compiler checks consistency, but a human decides which side (annotation or implementation) is wrong.
hints: What does the body DO with qty? Multiply — so its annotation must be number.
What does the body return? A concatenated string — so the return annotation must be string.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.instructions:
Export `priceLabel(cents: number, currency: string): string` producing:
- the amount as dollars with two decimals (divide by 100, use `toFixed(2)`)
- prefixed by the currency symbol: `'USD'` → `'$'`, `'EUR'` → `'€'`, anything else → the currency code plus a space
- negative amounts wrapped in parentheses WITHOUT a minus sign
Examples: `(1999, 'USD')` → `'$19.99'`; `(500, 'EUR')` → `'€5.00'`; `(500, 'SEK')` → `'SEK 5.00'`; `(-1250, 'USD')` → `'($12.50)'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/pri.explanation: A real formatting function has stages — normalize (abs), convert (cents to decimal string), decorate (symbol), wrap (negative styling) — and doing them in that order keeps each concern separate. The `let symbol: string` declaration shows annotation on a variable assigned across branches: TypeScript verifies every branch assigns a string before use.
hints: Take Math.abs(cents) first so toFixed never renders a minus sign.
Resolve the symbol with an if/else chain; declare it `let symbol: string` before the branches.
Decide on parentheses last, from the ORIGINAL sign of cents.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Which correctly declares an interface for `{ id: 7, title: "Hi" }`?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: An interface block lists `name: type;` members — no equals sign (that is `type` alias syntax). Option C is actually legal TypeScript (literal types!) but would accept ONLY id 7 and title "Hi", which is not what "an interface for posts" means.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: In `interface User { nickname?: string }`, what does the `?` mean for reading `user.nickname`?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: Optional means "may not be there", and the type system makes you face it: `user.nickname.toUpperCase()` is a compile error until you guard (`if (user.nickname)`) or default (`user.nickname ?? ""`). This converts the classic "undefined is not a function" runtime crash into a red squiggle.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: What does `readonly id: number` in an interface actually enforce?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: `readonly` lives entirely in the type system: `user.id = 5` won’t compile, which prevents whole classes of accidental mutation — but the emitted JavaScript has no protection, so code outside TypeScript (or using `any`) can still mutate. For runtime immutability you need `Object.freeze`.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Function `save(user: User)` expects `interface User { id: number; name: string }`. You call it with a variable holding `{ id: 1, name: "Ada", role: "admin" }`. What happens?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: Structural typing asks "does it have what User needs?" — extra properties on a variable are fine. (Passing a fresh object literal *directly* triggers stricter excess-property checking, a lint-like safeguard against typos.) Nothing is ever deleted; types don’t touch runtime values.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: The optional `tags` forces the guard: present for the mug (2 tags), absent for the lamp (the ternary falls to 0 rather than crashing on `undefined.length`). Interfaces are erased at runtime — what executes is just property access and a ternary.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: Shapes compose: `Customer` embeds `Address` by name, and the checker verifies the whole tree — `c.address.city` is known to be a string, so chaining `.toUpperCase()` is safe. "Ada — London E1" then "LONDON".
hints: Interfaces nest by referencing other interfaces.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Define an interface `Person { first: string; last: string }` and export `fullName(p: Person): string` returning `'<first> <last>'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: The interface turns a loose convention ("pass me something with first and last") into a checked contract. Every property read in the body is verified against it — rename `last` to `surname` in the interface and the compiler lists every line to update.
hints: Two string members in the interface; one template literal in the body.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Define `User { id: number; name: string; nickname?: string }` and export `displayName(u: User): string` returning the nickname when present, otherwise the name.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: The optional property and `??` are made for each other: the type system says "this might be undefined", and nullish coalescing is the one-token answer. A missing nickname falls through to name; an empty-string nickname (weird but present) would be kept — exactly what `??` means.
hints: The ? makes nickname string | undefined — `??` picks the fallback.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Define `Product { name: string; priceCents: number; taxRate: number }` and export `priceWithTax(p: Product): number` returning the price with tax, rounded: `Math.round(priceCents * (1 + taxRate))`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: Both numeric fields come pre-checked, so the only concern left is the money rule (round once, at the end). In plain JS, a `priceCents: "1000"` from a JSON import would coerce into "10001.08"-style chaos; the interface makes that a load-time type error instead.
hints: One multiplication and one Math.round, reading both numeric members.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Define `User { id: number; username: string; active: boolean }` and export `makeUser(id: number, username: string): User` returning a new user with `active` defaulting to `true`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: A factory with a declared return type is self-verifying: forget `active` and the function no longer compiles, because the literal doesn’t satisfy `User`. This inverts the usual testing burden — the shape is proven at compile time, and tests only pin the VALUES.
hints: Return an object literal; shorthand `{ id, username }` works when names match.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Define `Account { id: number; email: string; verified: boolean }` and export `updateEmail(acc: Account, email: string): Account` returning a NEW account object with the new email and `verified` reset to `false` (changing email requires re-verification). Do not mutate the input.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: Spread-and-override is the immutable update idiom, and the return annotation keeps it honest: the result must still be a complete `Account`. The business rule riding along (re-verification on email change) is the kind of invariant that belongs in exactly one function like this.
hints: Spread the original, then override email and verified.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Define `Task { title: string; done: boolean; dueDate?: string }` and export `taskLine(t: Task): string` returning `'[x] <title>'` when done or `'[ ] <title>'` when not, appending `' (due <dueDate>)'` when dueDate is present. E.g. `{title:'ship', done:false, dueDate:'2024-04-01'}` → `'[ ] ship (due 2024-04-01)'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: Both conditional pieces resolve to strings before the final assembly — flat and readable versus one nested ternary. The optional `dueDate` again forces the presence check; the empty-string suffix is the neutral element that makes the final template unconditional.
hints: Build the checkbox and the optional suffix separately, then combine.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Define `Point { x: number; y: number }` and export `moveBy(p: Point, dx: number, dy: number): Point` returning a NEW point shifted by the deltas.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: Small immutable value types like Point are where interfaces feel most natural: the function is a pure transformation from one Point to another, trivially testable. Returning a new object (not `p.x += dx`) keeps the caller’s point untouched.
hints: Return a fresh object literal computed from the old one.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Define `Contact { name: string; email?: string; phone?: string }` and export `contactCard(c: Contact): string` returning the name, then `' · <email>'` if present, then `' · <phone>'` if present: `{name:'Ada', email:'a@x.io'}` → `'Ada · a@x.io'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: With two optional fields there are four shape combinations, and the collect-then-join pattern handles all of them without a single separator bug — the classic alternative (string concatenation with manual " · ") gets at least one combination wrong on the first try.
hints: Collect present parts into an array, then join — no separator bookkeeping.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Define `CartItem { sku: string; priceCents: number; qty: number }` and export `itemTotal(item: CartItem): number` returning `priceCents * qty`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: CartItem is the archetypal CRUD shape, and this one-liner is where JS carts go wrong: a qty arriving as the string "3" from a form multiplies fine but then `+= total` concatenates elsewhere. With the interface, string quantities are stopped at the boundary where the object is first typed.
hints: One multiplication of two interface members.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Define `Progress { done: number; total: number }` and export `progressPercent(p: Progress): number` returning the percentage complete rounded with `Math.round` — and `0` when total is `0`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: Types eliminate the wrong-kind bugs but not the wrong-value ones: `total: 0` is a perfectly typed input that still needs the runtime guard against NaN. Interface for shape, guard for values — both layers, every time.
hints: Guard the zero-total case first — 0/0 is NaN, not an error.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Define `Book { title: string; author: string; year: number }` and export `bookLabel(b: Book): string` returning `'<title> by <author> (<year>)'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: Formatting functions that take the whole typed object (rather than three loose parameters) stay stable as the shape grows: add a `subtitle` to Book and this signature doesn’t change, while a `(title, author, year)` parameter list would churn at every call site.
hints: One template literal reading all three members.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Why is `function save(user: object)` a poor annotation compared to `function save(user: User)`?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: `user: object` rules out primitives but that’s all: `user.name` is a compile error (the type has no known members), so code devolves into casts. A named shape gives you checked property access, autocompletion, and refactoring support — the actual value of TypeScript.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Your API returns JSON you cast as `User`. The server actually sent `{ id: "1" }` (a string id). What does TypeScript do?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: An interface is a compile-time *promise*, and casting JSON just asserts the promise without checking it. The classic production failure: everything compiles, then `user.id + 1` produces "11". At network/file/form boundaries, validate the shape at runtime; types take over from there inward.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions: Define `Settings { theme: string; fontSize: number }` and export `withTheme(s: Settings, theme: string): Settings` returning a new settings object with the theme replaced — the ORIGINAL object must be unchanged afterwards (the test checks!).
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: TypeScript can mark properties `readonly`, but plain interfaces don’t stop `s.theme = theme` — immutability here is a discipline the test enforces at runtime. The `{ ...s, theme }` shape is how React state updates, reducer transitions, and good API layers all produce "the same thing, but with one change".
hints: Spread, then override: `{ ...s, theme }`.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.instructions:
Define the shapes `Line { description: string; qty: number; unitCents: number }` and `Invoice { customer: string; lines: Line[]; taxRate: number }`, then export `invoiceTotal(inv: Invoice): { subtotalCents: number; taxCents: number; totalCents: number }`:
- subtotal = sum of `qty * unitCents` over the lines
- tax = `Math.round(subtotal * taxRate)`
- total = subtotal + tax
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/int.explanation: Nested shapes (`Invoice` containing `Line[]`) mirror how JSON actually arrives, and the checker follows the nesting: `line.qty * line.unitCents` is verified numeric two levels deep. The inline return type shows annotations don’t require named interfaces — though if several functions returned this triple, naming it (e.g. `Totals`) would be the next refactor. The money rules (integer cents, round once) now have compiler support end to end.
hints: An interface member can be an array of another interface: `lines: Line[]`.
Accumulate the subtotal in a loop (or reduce), then round the tax ONCE.
The return type is an inline object type — braces in the annotation position.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: At runtime, what is a TypeScript tuple like `["ada", 1200]`?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: Tuples compile to ordinary arrays; `Array.isArray` is true and `push` physically works (though the type checker scolds you). Like every type, the tuple-ness is erased — so data from JSON claiming to be a tuple deserves a runtime length check at the boundary.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Which two annotations declare "an array of numbers"?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: `number[]` and `Array<number>` are interchangeable spellings; most style guides prefer the bracket form. Careful with `[number]`: that is a TUPLE of exactly one number, not an array of any length.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: What does `[string, number]` promise that `(string | number)[]` does not?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: The tuple fixes both length and per-position types: `t[0]` is a string, `t[1]` is a number, `t[2]` is an error. The union array could be `[]`, `[1, 2, 3]`, or all strings — reading an element gives the mushy `string | number` requiring narrowing. Position-meaningful data wants tuples.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: `const ids: number[] = [1, 2]; ids.push('3');` — what happens?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: The element type governs every mutation method — push, unshift, splice, index assignment. This is the quiet superpower of typed arrays: a `number[]` stays homogeneous for its whole life, so downstream `ids.reduce((a, b) => a + b)` can never hit string concatenation.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Given `const words: string[]`, what is the type of `words.map(w => w.length)`?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: TypeScript tracks types through callbacks: inside the arrow, `w` is a string (inferred from the array), `w.length` is a number, so the mapped result is `number[]`. Transform pipelines stay fully typed without a single annotation — inference carries it all.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: map doubles each element (1800,3000,500), reduce sums the originals (2650), filter keeps the two prices ≥ 500. All three callbacks had their parameter type inferred from `number[]` — the annotations on `doubled` and `total` are documentation, not necessity.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: 17 ÷ 5 is quotient 3 remainder 2 — returned together as a tuple and destructured into two correctly-typed locals. The explicit pair at the end shows tuple indexing: `pair[0]` is known to be the string, `pair[1]` the number (3 + 2 = 5), printing "attempts: 5".
hints: divide returns quotient and remainder as a pair.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Export a function `sumAll(nums: number[]): number` that returns the sum of all numbers (0 for an empty array).
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: The `0` initial value does double duty: it makes the empty-array case return 0 instead of throwing, and it tells TypeScript the accumulator is a number. Because the input is `number[]`, the `sum + n` inside can never become string concatenation.
hints: reduce with initial value 0 — which also handles the empty array.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Export a function `longestWord(words: string[]): string` that returns the longest string (first wins on ties). Assume a non-empty array.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: The strictly-greater comparison (`>` not `>=`) is what implements "first wins on ties" — flip it and the last tie-winner is returned instead. Inside the loop, `w` is inferred as `string` from `string[]`, so `.length` is always legal.
hints: Track best-so-far; strictly-greater keeps the first on ties.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Export a function `evensOnly(nums: number[]): number[]` that returns a new array with only the even numbers, preserving order.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: filter preserves the element type — `number[]` in, `number[]` out — and never mutates the input. Note 0 and −2 pass: `0 % 2` and `-2 % 2` are both 0, so the predicate is sign-agnostic.
hints: filter with the n % 2 === 0 predicate.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Export a function `wordLengths(words: string[]): number[]` that maps each word to its length.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: The signature tells the story before the body does: strings become numbers. This type-changing map is the simplest case of a typed pipeline — the compiler verifies the callback really does produce the declared output element type.
hints: One map call.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Export a function `minMax(nums: number[]): [number, number]` that returns the tuple `[smallest, largest]`. Assume a non-empty array.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: The tuple return type is the headline: one call yields two related values with their positions documented — callers destructure `const [lo, hi] = minMax(...)`. A plain `number[]` return would compile too, but would promise nothing about length or order.
hints: Spread the array into Math.min and Math.max; return both in one array literal.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Export a function `splitName(full: string): [string, string]` that splits a two-word name on the space into a `[first, last]` tuple: `'Ada Lovelace'` → `['Ada', 'Lovelace']`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: `split` returns `string[]` — unknown length — so repacking the two pieces into an explicit tuple literal is what upgrades the type to `[string, string]`. The function boundary converts loose data into a precise shape, which is most of what typed code does.
hints: split gives a string[]; return the first two elements as a tuple literal.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Export a function `distance(a: [number, number], b: [number, number]): number` that computes the Euclidean distance between two `[x, y]` points: `([0,0], [3,4])` → `5`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: Coordinate pairs are the canonical tuple: `[number, number]` says "exactly x then y", where `number[]` would accept `[1]` or `[1,2,3]`. Destructuring in the parameter list (`([x1, y1]: [number, number], ...)`) would work too — same types, different style.
hints: Subtract per coordinate, then Math.sqrt(dx² + dy²).

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Export a function `entriesToObject(entries: [string, number][]): Record<string, number>` that converts an array of `[key, value]` tuples into an object: `[['a', 1], ['b', 2]]` → `{ a: 1, b: 2 }` (later duplicates overwrite earlier ones).
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: `[string, number][]` reads inside-out: an array of pairs — exactly what `Object.entries` produces and `Object.fromEntries` consumes (which is a one-line alternative solution). `Record<K, V>` is the standard type for dictionary-shaped objects; you will use it constantly for lookups and tallies.
hints: `for (const [key, value] of entries)` destructures each tuple.
`Record<string, number>` is the type for "object with string keys and number values".

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Export a function `countAbove(scores: number[], threshold: number): number` that counts how many scores are strictly greater than the threshold.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: filter-then-length is the idiomatic "count matching" one-liner. The boundary case (50 is not above 50) is pinned by a test because strictly-vs-inclusive is precisely the kind of spec detail types cannot express — tests and types cover different failure modes.
hints: filter then .length — or a loop with a counter.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Export a function `reverseCopy(items: string[]): string[]` that returns a NEW array with the elements in reverse order, leaving the input unchanged.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: `reverse` is one of the mutating array methods (with sort and splice), so the spread-copy guards the caller’s data. The types don’t catch mutation — `items.reverse()` compiles fine — which is why the no-mutation rule stays a convention tests must enforce.
hints: reverse() mutates — spread into a copy first.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Export a function `topN(scores: number[], n: number): number[]` that returns the `n` largest scores in descending order, without mutating the input.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: Copy-sort-slice is the leaderboard idiom. The descending comparator `b - a` trips people up (positive means "a after b"), and `slice(0, n)` gracefully handles n larger than the array — no bounds check needed.
hints: Copy, sort descending with (a, b) => b - a, slice the first n.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Export a function `indexPairs(words: string[]): [number, string][]` that pairs each word with its index: `['a', 'b']` → `[[0, 'a'], [1, 'b']]`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: An array of tuples — `[number, string][]` — is the typed version of what `Array.entries()` yields. The callback return annotation matters: without it TypeScript infers each `[i, w]` literal as `(number | string)[]` (a loose mixed array), which would not satisfy the declared tuple-array return type.
hints: map’s callback receives (element, index) — return them as a tuple.
Annotate the callback’s return as [number, string] so the literal is read as a tuple, not a mixed array.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions: Export `swapPair(pair: [string, number]): [number, string]` returning the elements in reverse order — the RETURN tuple type is reversed too.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: Tuples track types per position, so swapping values swaps types: the signature `[string, number] → [number, string]` *is* the documentation. Returning `[pair[0], pair[1]]` by mistake would be a compile error — a reversed-order bug caught by the type checker alone.
hints: Index 1 first, index 0 second, in a new tuple literal.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.instructions:
Export `scoreboard(entries: [string, number][]): { winner: string; totalPoints: number; average: number }` for an array of `[playerName, points]` tuples:
- `winner`: the name with the highest points (first wins ties)
- `totalPoints`: sum of all points
- `average`: totalPoints / number of entries, rounded with `Math.round`
Assume at least one entry.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/arr.explanation: A single loop carries three pieces of state (total, best score, best name), demonstrating the tuple-heavy data flow of leaderboards and analytics: pairs in, summary object out. The destructuring loop head keeps the body readable, and every variable stays correctly typed without one annotation inside the function — the signature at the boundary did all the work.
hints: One pass can track the running total AND the best-so-far simultaneously.
Destructure each tuple in the loop head: for (const [name, points] of entries).
Strictly-greater (>) keeps the first winner on ties.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Which annotation says "fn takes a string and returns a number"?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: Function types mirror arrow syntax: parenthesized, annotated parameters, fat arrow, return type. The parameter NAME (`s`) is required in the type but purely documentary — `(input: string) => number` is the same type.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: What does a return type of `void` mean?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: `void` marks "nothing meaningful comes back" — loggers, event handlers, forEach callbacks. A bare `return;` is allowed. Assigning a void call’s result and using it is the mistake the annotation exists to flag.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Which function is correctly typed as returning `never`?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: `never` means control NEVER comes back normally: the function always throws (or loops forever). `fail` qualifies — every call ends in a throw. Returning undefined or falling off the end returns normally, which is `void` territory, not `never`.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Why is `function f(tag?: string, value: number)` rejected by the compiler?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: Arguments bind by position, so with an optional first slot, `f(5)` can’t tell whether 5 is the tag (wrong type) or the value (then what’s the tag?). Required-first ordering removes the ambiguity, which is why the rule exists in every language with optional parameters.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: In `function greet(name: string, greeting = 'Hello')`, what is the type of `greeting` and can callers omit it?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: A default value does two jobs: it makes the parameter optional AND lets its type be inferred (string, from ‘Hello’). Unlike `greeting?: string`, inside the body the type is plain `string` — the default has already filled the undefined hole for you.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Why is `callback: Function` considered the `any` of function types?
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: `Function` says "it’s callable" and nothing more: you can invoke it with the wrong arguments and use its result as anything. Spelling out the signature — `(item: string) => boolean` — is what makes callback-passing code actually safe.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: Applying the callback twice: 10 +3 +3 = 16, then 5 ×2 ×2 = 20. The arrows’ parameter `n` is contextually typed as number from the declared callback signature — no annotation needed at the call sites.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: Defaults fill from the left: box('hi') uses pad 1 and '*' → '* hi *'; box('hi', 3) overrides just pad → '*   hi   *'; the third call overrides both → '|hi|'. To override a later default you must supply the earlier ones — positional parameters have no skipping.
hints: Each call fills the defaults left to right.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Export `applyTwice(fn: (n: number) => number, n: number): number` that applies `fn` to `n`, then applies it again to the result.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: The function-type annotation documents and enforces the whole protocol: whatever callers pass must accept and return a number, so `fn(fn(n))` composes safely — the inner result is guaranteed to be valid input for the outer call.
hints: Nest the calls: fn(fn(n)).

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Export `countMatching(nums: number[], predicate: (n: number) => boolean): number` counting how many elements satisfy the predicate.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: A predicate parameter — `(n: number) => boolean` — is the most common callback shape in application code. Passing it directly to `filter` works because the types line up exactly; the compiler verifies that compatibility rather than you hoping.
hints: The predicate slots straight into filter.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Export `transformAll(words: string[], fn: (s: string) => string): string[]` applying `fn` to every element and returning the new array.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: This is `map` with the types written out loud — useful mostly as a reading exercise: the signature alone tells you everything the function can do. With both element types fixed to string, the callback can only be a string transformer.
hints: map takes the callback directly.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Export `buildUrl(host: string, path: string, port?: number): string`: return `'https://<host>:<port><path>'` when port is given, else `'https://<host><path>'`. E.g. `('api.example.com', '/users', 8080)` → `'https://api.example.com:8080/users'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: Inside the body, `port` is `number | undefined`, and the explicit `=== undefined` check narrows it — safer than truthiness, which would also treat port 0 as absent. Building the optional fragment separately keeps the final template linear.
hints: Check `port === undefined` — an optional parameter arrives as undefined when omitted.
Build the optional ":port" piece first, then one template literal.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Export `greetWith(name: string, greeting = 'Hello'): string` returning `'<greeting>, <name>!'`. Callers may omit the greeting.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: Compare with an optional `greeting?: string`: the default version keeps the body clean (greeting is always a string inside) and centralizes the fallback in the signature where readers see it. Prefer defaults over optionals whenever a sensible fallback exists.
hints: The default goes in the parameter list; the body never checks for undefined.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Export `joinWith(parts: string[], separator = ', '): string` joining the parts with the separator (default comma-space).
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: A thin typed wrapper over a builtin still adds value: the default separator becomes team policy in one place, and the signature advertises it. The inferred type of `separator` is string — defaults propagate types without annotations.
hints: Delegate to Array.prototype.join.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Export `makeMultiplier(factor: number): (n: number) => number` returning a function that multiplies its argument by `factor`. Note the RETURN type is itself a function type.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: Closures and types meet: the returned arrow closes over `factor` (JavaScript) while the annotation `(n: number) => number` types the product (TypeScript). The arrow’s `n` needs no annotation — the declared return type contextually types it.
hints: Return an arrow closing over factor; its parameter type is inferred from the declared return type.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Export `tallyWith(items: string[], score: (item: string) => number): number` that sums `score(item)` across all items.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: The callback here is a *projection* (string → number) rather than a predicate — the second great callback species. Separating "how to walk the data" (this function) from "how to value each item" (the callback) is the decomposition underlying map/reduce and most analytics code.
hints: Loop and accumulate — or reduce with the scorer inside.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Export `anyMatch(nums: number[], predicate: (n: number) => boolean): boolean` returning `true` when at least one element satisfies the predicate, stopping at the first hit.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: `some` is the existential quantifier with built-in short-circuiting, which the call-counting test verifies. Its sibling `every` is the universal one; together with filter/map/reduce they cover nearly all typed collection logic without manual loops.
hints: Array.prototype.some does exactly this, including the early exit.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Export `collectCalls(times: number, fn: (i: number) => string): string[]` calling `fn` with each index `0 .. times-1` and collecting the results in order.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: Generating N things from a function of the index is the typed version of "render N rows" — the callback receives the position and decides the content. The annotation `(i: number) => string` keeps the division of labor explicit.
hints: A classic indexed for loop pushing fn(i).

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Export `fail(message: string): never` that always throws `new Error(message)`, plus `firstOrFail(items: string[]): string` returning the first element — or calling `fail('empty list')` when the array is empty.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: Because `fail` is typed `never`, the compiler knows code after it is unreachable — so `firstOrFail` type-checks: on the empty path control provably never reaches the end, and on the other path a string is returned. Assertion helpers like this (`fail`, `assertNever`, `unreachable`) let you fail fast while keeping return types honest.
hints: fail’s entire body is one throw statement — that is what makes `never` accurate.
firstOrFail can return items[0] after the guard; the never-returning call satisfies the string return type on the empty path.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Export `compose(f: (n: number) => number, g: (n: number) => number): (n: number) => number` returning a NEW function that computes `f(g(n))` — g first, then f.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: Functions in, function out: all three positions share the `(n: number) => number` type, so composition is closed — you can compose compositions. The two tests pin the order convention (mathematical: compose(f, g) applies g first), the exact detail that bites when someone assumes pipeline order.
hints: Return an arrow: (n) => f(g(n)).
The "order matters" test distinguishes f(g(n)) from g(f(n)) — read it carefully.

bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.instructions: Export `filterMap(nums: number[], keep: (n: number) => boolean, transform: (n: number) => string): string[]` — in ONE pass over the input (a single loop), collect `transform(n)` for every element where `keep(n)` is true, preserving order.
bootforge/ts-basics/type-annotations/fun.explanation: Two differently-typed callbacks cooperate under one roof: the predicate gates, the transformer converts, and the declared types make it impossible to pass them in the wrong order (`(n) => boolean` is not assignable where `(n) => string` is expected). The single-pass requirement — enforced by counting transform calls — is the standard efficiency refinement over chaining filter().map(), worth knowing even though the chained version is fine for small arrays.
hints: One loop, one `if`, one push — not .filter().map(), which would be two passes (and the last test counts transform calls).
Annotate the accumulator: const out: string[] = [].
The two callbacks have different types: predicate returns boolean, transform returns string.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Which annotation accepts either a string or a number?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: The single pipe `|` builds union types. `||` is runtime-or (value syntax), `&` is an intersection ("both at once" — for primitives, an impossible type), and the bracket form is a tuple containing one of each.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Given `x: string | number`, why is `x.toUpperCase()` a compile error?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: The compiler must assume x could be either member at this point, so only the intersection of their capabilities is safe. To use string-only methods you first prove x is a string (`typeof x === "string"`) — which is exactly what narrowing means.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: What is the difference between `role: string` and `role: 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer'`?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: Each string literal is its own type, and the union enumerates the legal menu. Every assignment, comparison, and function argument is checked against it — the typo'd role, the status nobody handles, the sort order "ascending" vs "asc" mismatch: all caught before running.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: What does `user: User | null` communicate that `user: User` does not?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: With strict null checking, `User` means "definitely a user" and `User | null` means "maybe not found" — the single most valuable distinction in CRUD code. `findUser(id).name` is a compile error until you handle the null branch; the billion-dollar null crash becomes a red squiggle.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: With `type Status = 'pending' | 'active' | 'done'`, is `const s: Status = 'done'` legal? Is `const t: string = s`? Is `const u: Status = someString` (where someString: string)?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: Assignability flows from specific to general: the literal 'done' is a Status; every Status is a string. The reverse — any string into Status — is exactly the unsafe direction, because the string might be 'bananas'. That is why values entering from outside must be validated (checked against the menu) before being treated as Status.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: 'Ace' passes through, null falls back to 'ada42', and the empty string — being neither null nor undefined — is KEPT, so the last line prints just '!'. `??` applied to `string | null` collapses the type to string, and its value behavior matches: only the null member is replaced.
hints: ?? only replaces null/undefined — look closely at the third call.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: Concatenation stringifies either member: '#42' and '#a7f'. The literal-union variable holds 'pending', so the ternary prints 'in progress'. At runtime nothing remains of the union — just strings and a comparison.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: Each literal maps to its rank: high→3, low→1, medium→2, joining to '3,1,2'; then 3 + 3 = 6. Inside `rank`, after the first two ifs eliminate 'low' and 'medium', the compiler knows only 'high' remains — the bare `return 3` needs no condition.
hints: map each level through rank, then join.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Export a function `formatId(id: string | number): string` that returns the id prefixed with `'#'` — works for both union members since concatenation stringifies.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: This is the no-narrowing case: concatenation is valid for every member of the union, so the compiler allows it directly. Unions only force branching when you need member-specific behavior.
hints: No narrowing needed — + with a string works for both members.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Export a function `statusLabel(s: 'pending' | 'active' | 'done'): string` that maps each status to its display label: `'pending'` → `'Waiting'`, `'active'` → `'In progress'`, `'done'` → `'Complete'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: The parameter type IS the spec: no status outside the three can arrive, so the final `return` safely handles the only remaining literal. When a fourth status is added to the union later, this function keeps compiling but silently mislabels it — which is why the next lessons introduce exhaustive mappings.
hints: Three branches; after eliminating two literals, the third is certain.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Export a function `priorityRank(p: 'low' | 'medium' | 'high'): number` that returns 1 for low, 2 for medium, 3 for high.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: The lookup-object version has a hidden safety property: because `p` can only be one of the three literals, `ranks[p]` can never be undefined — the compiler verifies the object covers the union. Converting labels to sortable numbers like this is how "order tasks by priority" is implemented.
hints: A lookup object indexed by the literal is cleaner than an if-chain.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Export a function `toCents(v: string | number): number` that normalizes a price that may arrive as a number of cents or a numeric string: parse strings with `Number.parseInt(v, 10)`, pass numbers through.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: A taste of the next lesson: inside the `if`, TypeScript knows `v` is a string (parseInt accepts it); after it, only number remains (returned as-is). Normalizer functions like this sit at boundaries so the rest of the codebase deals in one type, not the union.
hints: typeof v === "string" narrows; in the other branch v is already a number.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Export a function `httpLabel(status: 200 | 404 | 500): string` that maps the NUMERIC literal union to text: 200 → `'OK'`, 404 → `'Not Found'`, 500 → `'Server Error'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: Literal types aren’t just for strings: `200 | 404 | 500` restricts a number to a menu the same way. An API layer typed with its actual status codes documents itself and rejects `httpLabel(418)` at compile time.
hints: Literal unions work with numbers too.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Export a function `triState(v: boolean | 'unknown'): string` that returns `'yes'` for `true`, `'no'` for `false`, and `'unknown'` for the literal `'unknown'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: Unions can mix kinds — a boolean and a string literal — to model tri-state data honestly, instead of the lying alternatives (null meaning "unknown", or a magic string "false"). Peel off the literal, and the leftover type is a clean boolean.
hints: Eliminate the string literal first; what remains is a plain boolean.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Export a function `firstDefined(primary: string | null, fallback: string): string` that returns `primary` unless it is `null`, in which case return `fallback`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: `??` is union-aware: applied to `string | null` it produces plain `string`, because the null member is consumed by the fallback. The empty-string test pins why `||` is wrong here — `''` is a real value the caller chose, and only `??` preserves it.
hints: ?? collapses the null member of the union.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Export a function `applySort(nums: number[], dir: 'asc' | 'desc'): number[]` that returns a NEW sorted copy — ascending or descending per the literal.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: The `'asc' | 'desc'` parameter is the typed version of the sanitize-sort allowlist from the JavaScript course: instead of validating at runtime that dir is one of two strings, the compiler guarantees it. Runtime validation is still needed where the value ENTERS the system (a query string) — but nowhere after.
hints: Copy first; pick the comparator by comparing dir to one literal.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Export a function `currencySymbol(code: 'usd' | 'eur' | 'gbp'): string` that maps the currency literal to its symbol: `'usd'` → `'$'`, `'eur'` → `'€'`, `'gbp'` → `'£'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: Compare with priceLabel from the previous module, which accepted `currency: string` and needed an else-branch for unknowns: the literal union deletes the unknown case entirely. Tightening a string parameter into a menu simplifies the body — fewer possible inputs, less handling.
hints: A three-entry lookup object indexed by the literal.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Export a function `toBytes(value: number, unit: 'kb' | 'mb' | 'gb'): number` that converts to bytes: kb × 1024, mb × 1024², gb × 1024³.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: Unit parameters are classic literal-union territory: `unit: string` would accept "KB", "kib", "kilobytes" and silently miss them all in a lookup. The three-literal menu makes the contract exact, and the factors table keeps the magic numbers in one labeled place.
hints: Lookup the factor, multiply.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Export a function `greetUser(name: string | null): string` that greets by name, or greets `'guest'` when name is null: `null` → `'Welcome, guest!'`, `'Ada'` → `'Welcome, Ada!'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: The `| null` member models "not signed in" honestly, and `??` resolves it inline at the display point. Anonymous-user fallbacks are the most frequent null-union you’ll meet in app code.
hints: ?? inside the template interpolation.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Export a function `sizeLabel(size: 's' | 'm' | 'l' | 'xl'): string` that expands the size code: `'s'` → `'Small'`, `'m'` → `'Medium'`, `'l'` → `'Large'`, `'xl'` → `'Extra Large'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: Code-to-label mappings are everywhere (sizes, countries, locales), and the pattern scales linearly: one table row per literal. Store the short code in the database, expand to the label at the display edge — the union type guards both ends of that journey.
hints: Lookup object again — four entries this time.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions: Export `normalizeIds(ids: (string | number)[]): number[]` converting every id to a number (`Number(id)` handles both members), skipping any that produce `NaN`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: Note the precedence trap called out in the hint — `(string | number)[]` vs `string | number[]` are wildly different types, and the parentheses are load-bearing. The body is a normalize-and-validate pipeline: convert each member uniformly, then filter out failures, producing the clean `number[]` the rest of the app wants.
hints: The parentheses matter: (string | number)[] is an array of either; string | number[] would be "a string, or an array of numbers".
Number() converts both members; validate with Number.isNaN before keeping.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.instructions:
Export `formatCell(value: string | number | boolean | null): string` for rendering a table cell:
- `null` → `'—'` (an em dash)
- booleans → `'yes'` / `'no'`
- numbers → the number with `toFixed(2)`
- strings → unchanged
Check the cases in an order that narrows correctly (null first!).
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/uni.explanation: A four-member union handled by successive elimination: each branch returns for one member, and the compiler tracks what’s left, so the final `return value` is provably a string. The zero test is the design lesson: branching on TYPE (`typeof value === "number"`) treats 0 as a number to format, where truthiness-based code (`value ? ... : "—"`) would wrongly render 0, false, and "" all as the dash.
hints: Four branches, one per union member; each check eliminates a member from the remaining type.
null must be checked with === null (typeof null is "object", useless here).
After the first three returns, only string remains — return it bare.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Inside `if (typeof v === 'string') { ... }` where `v: string | number`, what is the type of `v` in the branch — and after the if-block (given the branch returns)?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: Narrowing works by elimination along control flow: the branch proves string, and because that branch returns, code after it can only be reached with a number. The compiler performs this flow analysis statement by statement — it is reading your ifs as proofs.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: For `v: { radius: number } | { width: number; height: number }`, which check narrows to the circle shape?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: Both members are plain objects, so `typeof` says 'object' for either; `instanceof` needs classes. The `in` operator asks which properties exist — `'radius' in v` proves the circle member. (Reading `v.radius` before narrowing is itself a compile error: the property doesn't exist on the other member.)

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Narrowing `s: string | null` with `if (s) { ... }` — what is the trap?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: `if (s)` eliminates null AND `''` (and for numbers, 0 and NaN). Often that’s fine; when the falsy values are real data — an empty draft, a zero quantity — it silently misroutes them. The explicit `!== null` narrows exactly one member and nothing else.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Why does `typeof v === 'object'` fail to cleanly narrow `v: { id: number } | null | number[]` to the object member?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: JavaScript's oldest wart carries into narrowing: `typeof null` and `typeof []` are both 'object', so the check leaves `{ id: number } | null | number[]` barely narrowed. Order the checks by distinctiveness: `=== null` first, `Array.isArray` second — the plain object falls out as the remainder.

Control-flow analysis follows returns: any code after the guard can only execute when `s !== null`, so the type narrows for the whole remainder. Guard clauses at the top of a function — the style you used for validation in JavaScript — are also the cleanest *narrowing* style.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: The `in` check routes by structure: the dog prints 'woof', the car prints 'beep x4'. After the dog branch returns, `thing` is narrowed to Car, so `.horn` and `.wheels` are both safely available without any further check.
hints: 'bark' in thing picks the Dog branch.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: Three members, three routes: the string's length (5), the array's length times ten (30), and the object's count (42). Each check both decides at runtime AND narrows at compile time — one mechanism serving both worlds.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: Explicit `=== null` separates 'missing' from 'empty' — two states a truthiness check would merge. After the null check, `s.length` is safe (s: string), and the `''` case gets its own honest label. CRUD apps live on this distinction: no bio vs blank bio.
hints: null and the empty string take different paths — that is the point.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Export a function `double(v: string | number): string | number` that doubles either way: numbers → `v * 2`, strings → the string concatenated with itself.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: The same expression `v + v` means arithmetic in one branch and concatenation in the other — narrowing is what lets each branch use its member’s semantics safely. Without the check, `v * 2` would be a compile error on the string member.
hints: typeof narrows; in the second branch v is certainly a string, so + concatenates.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Export a function `lengthOf(v: string | string[]): number` that returns the character count of a string or the element count of an array.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: A deliberately sneaky case: `.length` exists on BOTH members, so `return v.length` compiles without narrowing — the union rule is "common operations allowed". The ternary with Array.isArray is shown for the pattern; recognizing when you don’t need it is equally valuable.
hints: Both members happen to have .length — but write the narrowing anyway (Array.isArray) to see it work; or note .length is common to both and allowed directly.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Export a function `sumFlexible(v: number | number[]): number` that returns the number itself, or the sum of the array.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: "One or many" parameters are a common API kindness, and `Array.isArray` is the canonical way to split them. After the array branch returns, `v` is narrowed to plain `number` — the compiler knows reduce’s result and the bare `v` are both numbers.
hints: Array.isArray narrows to number[]; the other branch is already the answer.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Export a function `upperOrDefault(s: string | null, fallback: string): string` that returns the upper-cased string, or the fallback (unchanged) when `s` is null. The empty string is a valid input and upper-cases to itself.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: The third test is the whole lesson: `if (!s)` would send `''` to the fallback, but `''.toUpperCase()` is a perfectly good empty string. Narrow by the member you mean (`=== null`), not by falsiness, whenever falsy values are legitimate data.
hints: Narrow with === null, NOT truthiness — the empty-string test will catch you.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Export a function `area(shape: { radius: number } | { width: number; height: number }): number` that computes the area: circles (`radius`) → `Math.round(Math.PI * r * r)`, rectangles → `width * height`. Use the `in` operator to tell them apart.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: Two object shapes can’t be split by `typeof` (both say "object"), so you discriminate by what they contain: `'radius' in shape` proves the circle. Inside the branch `shape.radius` is legal; outside it, only the rectangle remains. This is shape-based dispatch without any class hierarchy.
hints: 'radius' in shape — the property name in quotes, then the in keyword.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Export a function `idOf(v: number | { id: number }): number` that accepts a raw id or an entity carrying one, returning the number either way.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: APIs often accept "the thing or its id" — this narrowing makes that ergonomic without sacrificing safety. One typeof check splits primitive from object, and each branch extracts the number its own way. (deleteUser(user) and deleteUser(user.id) both just work.)
hints: typeof handles the primitive member; the leftover must be the object.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Export a function `joinFlexible(v: string | string[]): string` that returns the string unchanged, or the array joined with `', '`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: Narrowing works in ternaries too — the true arm sees `string[]`, the false arm `string`. Normalizing one-or-many inputs to a single display string is a UI chore this pattern dispatches in one line.
hints: Array.isArray in a ternary is enough.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Export a function `firstOrSelf(v: string | string[]): string | null` that returns the string itself, the first element of a non-empty array, or `null` for an empty array.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: Two layers of care: the type-level narrowing (array vs string) and the value-level guard (empty vs not). The `string | null` return type then tells callers the truth — this function can come up empty, and they must handle it. Honest signatures propagate safety outward.
hints: Narrow to the array first, then handle its empty case explicitly.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Export a function `nameOf(v: string | { name: string }): string` that accepts a bare name or an object carrying one; returns the name either way.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: Twin of idOf from earlier, with a string payload: accept the value or its wrapper, normalize immediately. Functions this small are still worth writing — they concentrate the union handling so callers and deeper code never repeat it.
hints: typeof splits primitive from object.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Export a function `safeTrim(s: string | null | undefined): string` that trims the string, or returns `''` for null/undefined.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: `(s ?? '')` narrows the three-member union to plain string in one expression — then `.trim()` is unconditionally safe. Collapse-then-operate often beats branch-per-member when all the empty members deserve identical treatment.
hints: Collapse both empty members with ?? first, then trim the guaranteed string.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Export a function `totalPoints(v: number | [number, number]): number` that returns the number itself, or the SUM of a `[base, bonus]` pair.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: `Array.isArray` narrows to the tuple, where indexes 0 and 1 are typed numbers. Unions of "simple value or richer structure" let APIs start simple and grow — old callers pass a number, new ones pass the pair, one function serves both.
hints: Array.isArray narrows to the tuple member.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Export a function `repeatText(text: string, times?: number): string` that repeats the text `times` times (no separator), defaulting to 2 when the parameter is omitted: `('ab')` → `'abab'`, `('ab', 3)` → `'ababab'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: An optional parameter IS a union (`number | undefined`), and resolving it to a definite local (`const n = times ?? 2`) right at the top is tidier than checking undefined at each use. (A default parameter `times = 2` would express this even better — both are idiomatic.)
hints: times is number | undefined inside — ?? gives it a value before use.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions: Export `classify(v: string | number | boolean | null | string[]): string` returning: `'null'`, `'boolean'`, `'number'`, `'list of N'` (N = array length), or `'text of N'` (N = string length) — narrowing in a safe order.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: A five-member union dispatched entirely by elimination, with the checks ordered so each is unambiguous: null before anything (its typeof lies), primitives by typeof, arrays by isArray, and the string earns the no-check remainder slot. The falsy probes (false, 0, "") in the tests would each break a truthiness-based version — type-driven branching is the robust default.
hints: null first (it would pollute typeof object checks), then the primitives, then Array.isArray, leaving string as the remainder.
false and 0 must classify by TYPE — any truthiness shortcut fails those tests.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.instructions:
Spreadsheet data arrives messy. Export `totalColumn(cells: (number | string | null)[]): number` summing the column:
- numbers count as themselves
- strings are parsed with `Number.parseFloat`; unparseable strings (NaN) are skipped
- `null` cells are skipped
E.g. `[10, '5.5', null, 'n/a', 4]` → `19.5`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/nar.explanation: Real import pipelines look exactly like this: per-element narrowing (null / number / string each handled on their own terms) plus per-value validation (the NaN check) — types route the members, guards judge the values. One unguarded `total += Number.parseFloat("n/a")` would turn the entire sum into NaN silently; the skip-invalid policy keeps the aggregate meaningful, which is a deliberate business decision the tests document.
hints: Narrow per element inside the loop: null first, then typeof number, leaving string.
After parsing, validate with Number.isNaN before adding — "n/a" must not poison the total.
continue keeps the branches flat.
