bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: What does `as const` change about `const config = { mode: 'dark' }`?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: TypeScript normally widens property values to their general type (string), assuming you might reassign. `as const` opts into exact literal types plus readonly — which is what lets a lookup table's values satisfy a literal-union type. (Runtime freezing still requires Object.freeze.)

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: A ticket status is typed `'open' | 'in-progress' | 'closed'` instead of `string`. Which bug class disappears?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: Every assignment and comparison is checked against the menu: the typo'd write, the `if (status === 'done')` against a state that doesn't exist in this app, the API handler missing a case — all surface at compile time. Runtime values from outside still need validation once, at the boundary.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Why prefer a transition TABLE (`{ draft: "review", ... }`) over an if/else chain for a state machine?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: With `Record<Status, Status>`, forgetting a row is a compile error — an if-chain just silently falls through. The table is also readable as a specification and testable as data. Branch logic for *decisions*, lookup tables for *mappings* is a good division.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: How does the const-object pattern (`const ROLES = {...} as const`) relate to TypeScript’s `enum` keyword?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: `enum` generates extra JavaScript and has quirks (numeric enums accept any number in older versions). The const object + literal union achieves the same modeling with zero runtime surprise — the values are just strings/numbers you can see. Know both; reach for the object first.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: A table is typed `Record<Status, string>` where Status has four members. You add a fifth member to Status. What happens to the table?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: Exhaustiveness is the superpower of `Record<UnionType, V>`: the type demands a value for EVERY member. Growing the union breaks every incomplete table at compile time — turning "find all the places that handle statuses" from a grep-and-pray exercise into a checklist of compiler errors.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: Two parallel Records share the same key union, so they can never disagree about which severities exist. Iteration follows the array: X=1, i=4, !=2. Keeping related lookups keyed by one union is how dashboards keep icons, colors, and counts in sync.
hints: Walk the levels array in its given order.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: Each lookup advances the state: draft → review → published, and the terminal state maps to itself, so the third step prints published again. A self-loop on terminal states is the standard trick for making "advance" total — it never needs an error case.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: The const object doubles as data and type source: `keyof typeof ROLES` derives the union ‘viewer’ | ‘editor’ | ‘admin’ from the object itself, so the menu lives in ONE place. Viewer (1) can’t edit, editor (2) and admin (3) can, and 3 − 1 = 2.
hints: Compare the numeric levels: editing needs level >= 2.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Export a function `nextStatus(s: 'draft' | 'review' | 'published'): 'draft' | 'review' | 'published'` that advances one step: `'draft'` → `'review'`, `'review'` → `'published'`, `'published'` → `'published'` (terminal). Use a lookup table, not an if-chain.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: The assignment in the prompt — publish buttons, review queues — is a state machine, and the table is its entire definition. `Record<Status, Status>` makes omitting a row a compile error, so the machine can never be asked to advance from a state it doesn’t know.
hints: Record<Status, Status> forces the table to cover all three states.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Export a function `canTransition(from: 'todo' | 'doing' | 'done', to: 'todo' | 'doing' | 'done'): boolean` that allows only forward moves and no-ops: todo→doing, doing→done, plus any state to itself. Everything else (including backwards) is false.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: Mapping the literals onto numbers turns transition rules into arithmetic: forward-by-one or stay. The kanban no-skipping, no-backsliding policy compresses to one expression — and changing the policy later means changing math, not re-enumerating pairs.
hints: Map each column to a number; legal moves advance by exactly 0 or 1.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Export a function `nextLight(light: 'red' | 'green' | 'yellow'): 'red' | 'green' | 'yellow'` that cycles the traffic light: red → green → yellow → red.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: Unlike the publishing machine (which parks at a terminal state), this one cycles — the table expresses either topology with equal ease, which is the advantage of rules-as-data. The type system guarantees the cycle is total: every light has a successor.
hints: Same table shape as nextStatus, but the last state wraps around.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Export a function `hasAtLeast(role: 'viewer' | 'editor' | 'admin', required: 'viewer' | 'editor' | 'admin'): boolean` that returns whether `role` meets or exceeds `required`, with viewer < editor < admin.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: Role hierarchies are ordered menus, and the numeric mapping makes "at least editor" one comparison instead of enumerating allowed pairs. Every authorization middleware you will ever write contains this exact function under some name.
hints: Map roles to numeric levels; compare with >=.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Export a function `directionDelta(dir: 'north' | 'south' | 'east' | 'west'): [number, number]` that returns the `[dx, dy]` movement tuple: north `[0, 1]`, south `[0, -1]`, east `[1, 0]`, west `[-1, 0]`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: Literals, tuples, and Records compose: the table’s value type `[number, number]` keeps each delta a proper coordinate pair. Game movement, grid navigation, and cursor logic all reduce to look-up-the-delta — and the compiler insists all four directions exist.
hints: A Record mapping each literal to its tuple.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Export a function `planPriceCents(plan: 'free' | 'pro' | 'team'): number` that returns the monthly price in cents: free 0, pro 900, team 2900.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: Pricing tables are the friendliest introduction to Record types: when marketing adds a `business` plan to the union, every `Record<Plan, ...>` in the codebase fails to compile until it has a row — the compiler walks you to each place needing a decision.
hints: Record<Plan, number> — the compiler demands a price for every plan.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Export a function `toggleArchive(state: 'active' | 'archived'): 'active' | 'archived'` that flips between the two states.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: A two-literal union is the typed boolean-with-names: `'active' | 'archived'` reads better in data and logs than true/false, and the toggle stays one expression. Archive/unarchive endpoints are literally this.
hints: One ternary — a two-state machine is just a toggle.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Export a function `gradePoints(grade: 'A' | 'B' | 'C' | 'D' | 'F'): number` that returns the GPA points: A 4, B 3, C 2, D 1, F 0.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: Another code-to-number mapping — notice how mechanical these have become: union for the menu, object for the mapping, one indexed return. That sameness is the point; a new fixed-menu requirement should take two minutes, not a design meeting.
hints: Five-row lookup table.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Export a function `opposite(dir: 'north' | 'south' | 'east' | 'west'): 'north' | 'south' | 'east' | 'west'` that returns the opposite compass direction.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: A self-inverse mapping (apply it twice and you’re back) expressed as data — easy to verify by reading, impossible to leave incomplete thanks to the Record type. "Undo a move" and "go back" features live on functions like this.
hints: A Record<Direction, Direction> that pairs each with its inverse.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Export a function `statusColor(s: 'ok' | 'degraded' | 'down'): string` that maps a service status to a display color: `'ok'` → `'green'`, `'degraded'` → `'yellow'`, `'down'` → `'red'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: Status pages, health dashboards, uptime monitors: the status-to-color map is their beating heart, and centralizing it means the whole UI repaints consistently when design changes yellow to orange. One table, one truth.
hints: Three-row lookup.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Export a function `movePoint(p: [number, number], dir: 'north' | 'south' | 'east' | 'west'): [number, number]` that moves the `[x, y]` point one step: north `y+1`, south `y-1`, east `x+1`, west `x-1`, returning a NEW tuple.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: Composition of two earlier exercises: look up the delta (literal union → tuple), then apply it (tuple arithmetic into a fresh tuple). Larger features are mostly this — previously-built small pieces snapped together, with types verifying the joints.
hints: Reuse the delta-table idea, destructure the delta, add component-wise.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions: Export `isTerminal(s: 'open' | 'resolved' | 'closed' | 'wontfix'): boolean` — `true` for the states where work is finished: `'closed'` and `'wontfix'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: Classifying a subset of the menu (terminal vs active states) as a named array keeps the policy in one place and typed: only real IssueStates can appear in TERMINAL. Issue trackers branch on exactly this predicate for "can comment?", "show reopen button?", and archival sweeps.
hints: An array of the terminal literals plus .includes — or two === comparisons.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.instructions:
Model an order lifecycle. With `type OrderStatus = 'cart' | 'placed' | 'paid' | 'shipped' | 'cancelled'`, export `applyEvent(status: OrderStatus, event: 'checkout' | 'pay' | 'ship' | 'cancel'): OrderStatus`:
- `checkout`: cart → placed
- `pay`: placed → paid
- `ship`: paid → shipped
- `cancel`: allowed from cart, placed, or paid → cancelled
- any event not valid for the current status returns the status UNCHANGED (shipped and cancelled accept nothing)
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/lit.explanation: The two-level table IS the business specification — you can read the entire order policy (can't cancel after shipping, can't pay twice) from the data without tracing a single branch. `Partial<...>` is the key type tool: inner maps list only legal events, and the `?? status` fallback converts every gap into a safe no-op. When product adds a 'refund' event, the type of TRANSITIONS forces a conscious decision for each status. This table-driven state machine is the single most transferable pattern in this course — orders, tickets, documents, deployments all want it.
hints: A nested table: per status, a map of allowed events to the resulting status.
Partial<Record<OrderEvent, OrderStatus>> lets each status list only ITS legal events.
The no-op rule falls out of `lookup ?? status` — a missing entry means stay put.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.instructions: You need to name the union `'draft' | 'published'`. Which declaration works?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.explanation: `type` can name ANY type: unions, tuples, primitives, functions, objects. `interface` describes only object/function shapes — there is no interface syntax for a union. This is the clearest rule in the type-vs-interface debate: unions always mean `type`.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.instructions: How do `interface Admin extends User { level: number }` and `type Admin = User & { level: number }` relate?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.explanation: For everyday shape composition they are interchangeable: an Admin has every User field plus `level`. (Edge cases differ — extends errors earlier on conflicting members, interfaces can merge declarations — but the mental model "combine these shapes" covers both.)

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.instructions: For a plain object shape like `User { id: number; name: string }`, which should you use?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.explanation: Both declare the shape identically for everyday purposes. The genuine differences (declaration merging, extends ergonomics vs union capability) rarely matter for app code — but a codebase that mixes them randomly is harder to read than one that chose either.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.instructions: Where should the `Post` type used by five modules of a blog app live?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.explanation: Types export and import exactly like values (`export type Post = ...` / `import type { Post }`). Five copies WILL drift — someone adds `updatedAt` to three of them — and the compiler can’t warn because each copy is internally consistent. One exported definition makes the shape an actual contract.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.instructions: What does `import type { Post } from "./types.js"` do differently from a normal import?
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.explanation: `import type` promises the import exists only for the checker: compiled JavaScript contains no trace of it, which avoids loading a module (and its side effects) purely for its shapes. For plain type sharing either form works, but `import type` states intent and keeps the module graph lean.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.explanation: A typed collection filtered by a literal-union field: two published posts survive, and their titles join to "Hello & Types". The `p.status === "published"` comparison is checked against the union — compare against "live" (not a member) and the compiler flags it.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.instructions: Using `type Post = { id: number; authorId: number; title: string; body: string; status: 'draft' | 'published' }`, export `createPost(id: number, authorId: number, title: string): Post` — new posts start with an empty body and status `'draft'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.explanation: The factory encodes creation policy (drafts, empty body) in one checked place — the `: Post` return type means forgetting a field or typo’ing a status won’t compile. Every entity in a CRUD app deserves exactly one such factory.
hints: Return a literal with the defaults filled in; the return type checks completeness.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.instructions: With the same `Post` type (status `'draft' | 'published'`), export `publishPost(post: Post): Post` returning a NEW post object with status `'published'` (input unmutated).
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.explanation: Status changes as pure functions — old object in, new object out — make audit trails and undo trivially possible, and the literal-union status means the override can only be a legal state. Publishing an already-published post is a harmless no-op by design here.
hints: Spread and override status.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.instructions: With `type Post = { id: number; authorId: number; title: string }` (trimmed for this exercise), export `postsByAuthor(posts: Post[], authorId: number): Post[]` returning that author's posts in order.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.explanation: `authorId` is a foreign key in miniature — the filter is the in-memory version of `WHERE author_id = ?`. Typing both sides as number prevents the classic bug where one side is the string "10" and the comparison silently never matches.
hints: One filter on the foreign key.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.instructions: With `type User = { id: number; username: string }`, export `findUser(users: User[], id: number): User | null` — the user, or `null` when absent (not undefined).
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.explanation: The `User | null` return is the honest lookup signature: callers are forced to handle the miss. Normalizing `find`’s undefined to null (`?? null`) keeps one consistent "absent" value across the API — mixing null and undefined in return types breeds subtle bugs.
hints: Array.find yields undefined on miss — convert with ?? null.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.instructions: With `type Comment = { id: number; postId: number; author: string; text: string }`, export `addComment(comments: Comment[], comment: Comment): Comment[]` returning a NEW array with the comment appended (input unmutated).
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.explanation: The immutable-append one-liner, now typed: only complete `Comment` objects can enter the array, so a comment missing its postId never gets stored. `[...old, item]` over `push` is the default in state-managed UIs where object identity signals change.
hints: Spread the old array, append the new element.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.instructions: With the same `Comment` type, export `commentCountByPost(comments: Comment[]): Record<number, number>` mapping each postId to its comment count.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.explanation: The familiar count-into-an-object pattern gains a typed container: `Record<number, number>` documents that keys are post ids and values are counts. This is `GROUP BY post_id, COUNT(*)` in memory — the aggregation every post list page needs for its "N comments" badges.
hints: The counting pattern, typed: Record<number, number> and ?? 0.

bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.instructions: With `type Post = { id: number; title: string; body: string }`, export `excerpt(post: Post, maxLen: number): string` — the body unchanged when within `maxLen`, else the first `maxLen` characters plus `'…'`.
bootforge/ts-basics/unions-narrowing/typ.explanation: Truncation for list views — the boundary test (exactly maxLen passes untouched) is the detail that separates a correct implementation from one that appends a pointless ellipsis to content that already fits. Types ensure a Post arrives; the logic handles the rest.
